summary: A protocol analysis report on extensions to RIP for demand circuits, documenting key features and implementation experience, as required by the Routing Protocol Criteria.

eli5.summary: A report card on a plan to stop a routing chatterbox from dialing a phone line all day just to say nothing changed.

questions: how does demand rip reduce costs
subtitle: Using RIP on dial-up networks without constant polling

tldr.problem: RIP sends periodic routing updates at regular intervals, which is wasteful and expensive on wide-area networks with dial-up links where every minute of connection costs money.
tldr.mechanism: Demand RIP changes the protocol to send routing updates only when something actually changes (triggered updates), and uses an underlying circuit manager to establish connections only when needed rather than keeping them always open.
tldr.outcome: RIP can now work cost-effectively on switched networks like X.25 and ISDN, while still maintaining compatibility with standard RIP on local networks.

facts.label: Network types supported
facts.value: X.25, ISDN, point-to-point links with PPP

facts.label: Compatibility
facts.value: Works with standard RIP on LANs

facts.label: Implementations known at publication
facts.value: One completed (Spider Systems), two in development

today: RFC 1582 defines the actual Demand RIP extensions; this RFC documents them. Though dial-up networks have largely been replaced by always-on broadband, the pattern of triggered updates is still used in modern routing protocols.

sections.title: RIP and the Demand Circuit Problem
sections.content:
Standard RIP (Routing Information Protocol) sends periodic routing updates at fixed intervals. This works fine on local area networks where the link is always available and bandwidth is plentiful, but on wide-area networks using switched circuits like X.25 packet networks or ISDN, every connection costs money. A router that sends routing updates every 30 seconds across a switched line will incur continuous costs even when the network is stable and no changes need to be communicated.

This RFC documents how extensions to RIP can make it practical for dial-up and switched WAN links. Instead of periodic broadcasting, Demand RIP sends updates only when the routing database changes.
sections.eli5: A postcard says the same thing every minute whether anything changed or not. A smarter system waits until it has real news to share.

sections.title: How Demand RIP Works
sections.content:
Demand RIP introduces four key mechanisms. Triggered updates replace periodic broadcasts: updates are sent only when something in the routing database changes, and they are retransmitted until acknowledged. The packet format includes sequence and fragment numbers to track delivery.

A circuit manager runs below the network layer and controls when connections are made. When a router has data or a routing update to send, the circuit manager establishes a connection to the peer. After inactivity, the circuit closes automatically. If the circuit manager detects the line is down, it signals this to the routing application.

Presumption of reachability means that in a stable network, if no updates are being received on a circuit, the router assumes the most recent information is still valid and the path is still working. This avoids the need to poll. When the circuit manager detects the path is truly down, only then does the routing information time out.

Finally, flow control prevents the router from sending updates when the circuit is down, and optionally rate-limits update transmission to avoid overwhelming the circuit.
sections.eli5: The circuit manager is like a receptionist who only opens the office door when there is business to do, and closes it when things are quiet. Routes are assumed still good unless we hear they are broken.

sections.title: Implementation and Limits
sections.content:
At the time this RFC was written, Spider Systems had completed an implementation supporting RIP-1 and IPX RIP on X.25 and ISDN networks, and it interoperated with standard RIP implementations on Ethernet LANs. Two other Novell-only implementations were in development.

Demand RIP does have restrictions. It requires the ability to place calls in both directions; some dial-up services allow calls in only one direction. It also cannot work with third-party advertisement of routes on the WAN—the next-hop address in RIP-2 advertisements must be 0.0.0.0 on a demand circuit.
sections.eli5: The system works when both sides can call each other, and when routes are announced from the actual router sending the update.

sections.title: Security on Demand Links
sections.content: The circuit manager matches incoming call requests against a list of approved physical addresses. The routing application checks the logical address of incoming updates. This two-layer authentication prevents unauthorized routers from sending updates across the WAN. RIP-2 authentication can provide an additional layer of security where needed.
sections.eli5: The phone number and the sender's address must both match a trusted list before the router listens to an update.
